name: 京都千丸 しゃかりき 本店 (Kyoto Senmaru Shakariki Honten)

claims.text: As a tsukemen and ramen shop, the dipping tare is virtually certain to be standard wheat-based Japanese soy sauce, and the noodles are wheat flour; no gluten-free preparation is indicated.

The broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and dried-fish (niboshi) double soup; all bowls are animal-based with no listed vegetarian or vegan option, and shared broth/equipment makes cross-contact unavoidable.

name: 京都担担麺 金鵄楼 本店 (Kyoto Tantanmen Kinshiro Honten)

claims.text: Tantanmen tare is typically made with wheat-containing soy sauce; no allergen breakdown is published for this shop, so wheat should be assumed present in the sauce as well as the noodles.
The broth is sesame-rich and bowls are topped with pork meat miso; no separate vegetarian/vegan preparation is described.
Shared kitchen turning out wheat noodles (udon, soba, ramen, yakisoba), tempura and curry; no gluten-free handling indicated, so high cross-contamination risk for celiac diners.
The chuka-soba is a chicken-bone soy (shoyu) broth; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat and no gluten-free tare is offered.
Broths and dishes rely on chicken-bone stock, dashi, pork, fish cake and egg; no vegan preparation indicated.

name: 麺ビストロ Nakano (Men Bistro Nakano)

claims.text: The signature bowls are white and black shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen, and shoyu tare in Japan is virtually always made with wheat-containing soy sauce; treat the tare as a wheat source.
Broths lean on chicken stock and Japanese fish dashi (節), and several signature noodles are cream/dairy-based potages, so vegan cross-contact is inherent to the kitchen, not just incidental.
Table-only seating in a calm, bistro-style room with small plates and wine makes for an easy, unhurried meal, though the menu itself is not built around dietary restrictions.

name: 麺ショップ この味出来太蔵 (Men Shop Kono Aji Dekitazo)

claims.text: The bowls are soy-forward (a soy-tare jiro and soy-based Chinese soba), and ramen tare is conventionally made with wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free tare is indicated.
All broths are animal-based (chicken-and-pork-bone), prepared in a single small kitchen alongside pork belly, chashu and karaage, so a plant-only request cannot be isolated.

name: 麺処 虵の目屋 (Mendokoro Janomeya)

claims.text: Bowls are served over the shop's own house-made Japanese wheat noodles, so wheat is intrinsic to every dish; there is no gluten-free option.
The signature 鶏そば is a soy-seasoned (醤油) chicken broth; standard Japanese shoyu tare contains wheat.
All broths are 100% chicken (gara, whole chicken, water) with chicken/duck chashu toppings; there is no meat-free preparation, so any bowl will contain animal products.

name: 麺飯食堂 てら田や (Menhan Shokudo Teradaya)

claims.text: Wheat ramen/chuka-soba noodles are the core product, boiled in shared water; the soy-based tare and seasonings almost certainly contain wheat. Not suitable for celiac diners.
Broth/tare is built on soy-based seasoning (chuka-soba shoyu profile), which in Japan is typically brewed with wheat.
Broth is pork clear soup plus fish/seafood dashi; bowls carry chashu, wonton and egg. No vegan options and pervasive animal stock.
Ramen here is wheat-noodle based and broths/tare are chicken and (for the soy version) wheat-soy-sauce based; no gluten-free handling is indicated anywhere.
The shoyu ('thick soy' / 鶏そば soy-style) bowls use soy sauce tare, which in a standard Japanese ramen-ya is wheat-based; no wheat-free tare is mentioned.
All broths are chicken-based and toppings include chicken char siu and roast pork; there are no plant-based options, so no meaningful vegan handling exists.
